interactions.label: Why is the reticulocyte production index preferred over the raw reticulocyte per

params.question: Why is the reticulocyte production index preferred over the raw reticulocyte percentage when evaluating bone marrow response in anaemia?

answers.text: It measures the absolute number of reticulocytes per microlitre, which is more precise than a percentage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The absolute reticulocyte count is a different measure. The RPI specifically corrects the percentage for the reduced red-cell denominator in anaemia.

answers.text: It corrects for the reduced red-cell mass that falsely elevates the raw reticulocyte percentage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In anaemia, fewer red cells circulate, shrinking the denominator and making the raw percentage appear falsely high. The RPI divides by the normal haematocrit (45) to give a true production rate.

answers.text: It adjusts for the patient's age and sex to provide a standardised value

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The RPI does not adjust for age or sex. It corrects the reticulocyte percentage by comparing the patient's haematocrit to the normal value of 45.

answers.text: It accounts for differences in reticulocyte size between microcytic and macrocytic anaemias

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Reticulocyte size is not part of the RPI calculation. The correction addresses the falsely inflated percentage caused by a reduced total red-cell count.

overallFeedback.feedback: The RPI corrects for the artificially inflated percentage caused by having fewer red cells in circulation. An RPI ≥ 2 signals adequate marrow response (haemolysis, blood loss), while < 2 signals inadequate response (deficiency, suppression).

Right. RPI = (reticulocyte % × patient haematocrit) ÷ 45. An RPI of 2 or above indicates hyperproliferation (haemolysis or blood loss), while below 2 indicates hypoproliferation (deficiency or marrow suppression).

interactions.label: Which combination of laboratory findings forms the diagnostic fingerprint of hae

params.question: Which combination of laboratory findings forms the diagnostic fingerprint of haemolytic anaemia?

answers.text: Low serum ferritin, high total iron-binding capacity, and low transferrin saturation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This pattern indicates iron deficiency anaemia, not haemolysis. In haemolysis, iron stores are typically normal or elevated because iron is recycled from destroyed red cells.

answers.text: Pancytopaenia with reticulocytopenia and a hypocellular bone marrow

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This pattern characterises aplastic anaemia — marrow failure. Haemolytic anaemia shows increased reticulocytes as the marrow compensates for accelerated red-cell destruction.

answers.text: Elevated reticulocyte count, raised LDH, low haptoglobin, and raised unconjugated bilirubin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Accelerated red-cell destruction releases LDH and free haemoglobin (which binds haptoglobin, lowering it). Unconjugated bilirubin rises from haem catabolism, and the marrow responds by releasing more reticulocytes.

answers.text: Macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils on peripheral smear

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This smear pattern is diagnostic of megaloblastic anaemia from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, reflecting impaired DNA synthesis rather than red-cell destruction.

overallFeedback.feedback: The haemolytic fingerprint is: elevated reticulocytes (marrow compensation), raised LDH and unconjugated bilirubin (from red-cell breakdown), and low haptoglobin (consumed by free haemoglobin). This combination distinguishes haemolysis from other causes of anaemia.

Right. These four markers — high reticulocytes, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, and raised unconjugated bilirubin — together confirm accelerated red-cell destruction and distinguish haemolysis from deficiency states and marrow failure.

interactions.label: A 52-year-old man presents with microcytic anaemia, low serum ferritin, and mela

params.question: A 52-year-old man presents with microcytic anaemia, low serum ferritin, and melaena. Iron deficiency anaemia is confirmed on laboratory work-up. What should be the primary clinical priority?

answers.text: Start oral ferrous sulphate and reassess haemoglobin in four weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Starting iron is appropriate but must not be the sole action. In a middle-aged man with melaena, gastrointestinal malignancy must be excluded even when a benign cause is apparent — the dangerous diagnosis hides behind the obvious one.

answers.text: Investigate for underlying gastrointestinal malignancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This is the safety-netting principle: iron deficiency is the haematological classification, but in a middle-aged man with melaena, GI malignancy is the diagnosis that cannot be missed. Iron replacement treats the effect; investigation targets the cause.

answers.text: Order haemoglobin electrophoresis to exclude thalassaemia trait

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A low ferritin already confirms iron deficiency. Thalassaemia trait shows normal or elevated ferritin. This test does not address the critical question of why a middle-aged man has iron deficiency with GI bleeding.

answers.text: Refer for immediate bone marrow aspiration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bone marrow aspiration is reserved for unexplained pancytopaenia, suspected infiltration, or refractory anaemia. Here the diagnosis is clear — the priority is identifying the source of bleeding.

overallFeedback.feedback: The safety-netting principle requires you to ask: what dangerous diagnosis could this presentation be hiding? Here, iron deficiency anaemia is confirmed, but melaena in a 52-year-old demands investigation for gastrointestinal malignancy — the cause behind the deficiency.

Right. Safety-netting ensures that the dangerous diagnosis hiding behind the obvious one is not missed. Iron deficiency explains the blood picture, but gastrointestinal malignancy explains the bleeding — and that is the diagnosis that cannot be missed.

interactions.label: In which of the following clinical scenarios is bone marrow aspiration most appr

params.question: In which of the following clinical scenarios is bone marrow aspiration most appropriately indicated?

answers.text: A young woman with microcytic anaemia and a serum ferritin of 5 ng/mL

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The low ferritin confirms iron deficiency anaemia. The diagnosis is clear from simpler tests, and bone marrow aspiration would add nothing to management. Start iron replacement.

answers.text: A patient with macrocytic anaemia showing a good reticulocyte response to vitamin B12 injections

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A rising reticulocyte count confirms the diagnosis and treatment response. Bone marrow aspiration is unnecessary when simpler tests have identified the cause and treatment is working.

answers.text: A patient with unexplained pancytopaenia that fails to respond to empirical therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Bone marrow aspiration is reserved for unexplained pancytopaenia, suspected marrow infiltration, or anaemia refractory to treatment. It is not a shortcut around interpreting simpler blood tests.

answers.text: A patient with normocytic anaemia, elevated ferritin, and active pulmonary tuberculosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This pattern — normocytic anaemia with elevated ferritin in active infection — is classic anaemia of chronic disease. The hepcidin-mediated mechanism is understood, and the diagnosis follows from the clinical and biochemical picture without marrow sampling.

overallFeedback.feedback: Bone marrow aspiration is reserved for specific situations: unexplained pancytopaenia, suspected infiltration, or refractory anaemia. When simpler tests — peripheral smear, iron studies, B12 and folate levels — can establish the diagnosis, marrow aspiration adds cost and discomfort without benefit.

Right. Bone marrow aspiration is a targeted investigation for specific indications — unexplained pancytopaenia, suspected marrow infiltration, or treatment-refractory anaemia. It should never replace systematic interpretation of the haemogram, smear, and iron studies.

interactions.label: A doctor at a primary health centre is planning an anaemia prevention programme

params.question: A doctor at a primary health centre is planning an anaemia prevention programme for school-going adolescents. Under the Anaemia Mukt Bharat programme, which supplementation schedule should be implemented?

answers.text: Daily iron and folic acid tablets for 100 consecutive days each year

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Daily supplementation under Anaemia Mukt Bharat is prescribed for pregnant women, not adolescents. Adolescents receive a weekly schedule to improve compliance in school-based programmes.

answers.text: Weekly iron and folic acid tablets

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Anaemia Mukt Bharat programme prescribes weekly iron and folic acid for adolescents, while pregnant women receive daily supplementation throughout pregnancy and for 180 days postpartum.

answers.text: Monthly intramuscular iron dextran injections

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Parenteral iron is reserved for individual patients with malabsorption or intolerance to oral iron. Population-level programmes use oral supplementation for feasibility and cost-effectiveness.

answers.text: Iron tablets only during confirmed anaemia episodes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Anaemia Mukt Bharat is a prophylactic programme targeting all adolescents regardless of haemoglobin status. Waiting for confirmed anaemia defeats the preventive purpose of the programme.

overallFeedback.feedback: The Anaemia Mukt Bharat programme prescribes weekly iron and folic acid tablets for adolescents and daily supplementation for pregnant women throughout pregnancy and for 180 days postpartum. The programme is prophylactic, targeting all individuals in these groups regardless of current anaemia status.

Right. Anaemia Mukt Bharat targets all life stages: weekly IFA for adolescents, daily IFA for pregnant women throughout pregnancy and 180 days postpartum. This prophylactic approach addresses the 57% anaemia prevalence among Indian women aged 15–49.
